articles.title: Weekly Digest Recovery Using FIFO Queue Webhook Deduplication and Idempotency Keys
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Put each active customer's weekly digest in a FIFO queue with a stable event ID, but treat its five-minute duplicate window as traffic filtering, not correctness. Before sending, atomically cla…
articles.body: TL;DR: Put each active customer's weekly digest in a FIFO queue with a stable event ID, but treat its five-minute duplicate window as traffic filtering, not correctness. Before sending, atomically claim that event ID in durable storage; acknowledge the message only after the send is recorded. Use a standard queue instead when ordering has no business value and delayed retries are the main requirement. The page is weekly_digest_duplicate_send_total > 0 . At 03:07, the on-call view should contain the digest event ID, customer ID, queue type, message attempt, first-seen time, claim result, and final disposition. A graph of total queue depth looks reassuring while one customer receives the same edition twice, so it is not the first screen I would trust.
articles.author: BrodyVance2149

articles.title: Node.js Media Renewal Jobs: At-Least-Once Replay Governance for Duplicate Processing
articles.excerpt: A media subscription renewal reminder has a deadline, and the queue does not know about it. The queue only knows delivery. With an at-least-once background job queue, retries and duplicate jobs are no…
articles.body: A media subscription renewal reminder has a deadline, and the queue does not know about it. The queue only knows delivery. With an at-least-once background job queue, retries and duplicate jobs are normal; the engineering decision is how replay is governed so one renewal cycle creates one reminder intent. Short answer: make replay a recorded business decision. Derive one idempotency key from the renewal cycle, store the decision and outbound intent together, and route every later delivery through that record. Acknowledging a message is not evidence that the reminder happened. This framing matters during incidents. A consumer can disappear after committing storage but before acknowledging its delivery.
articles.author: BartholomewVance6831

articles.title: Showing license expiry in the right time zone
articles.excerpt: A support ticket arrives: a customer in Auckland says your app reports their license as expired today, but their renewal receipt clearly says it runs through the end of the month. You check the key. I…
articles.body: A support ticket arrives: a customer in Auckland says your app reports their license as expired today , but their renewal receipt clearly says it runs through the end of the month. You check the key. It is signed, it is theirs, and the expiry instant is comfortably in the future. Then a second customer, in Los Angeles, with the same expiry on their key, reports no problem at all — their copy says "expires tomorrow." Nothing is wrong with either license. Your UI rendered one instant onto two different calendars. This is not the clock-skew problem, where two machines honestly disagree about what time it is , and it is not an attacker rolling the clock back . Both clocks here are correct. The bug is in how Keyright 's expiry — a UTC instant — gets turned into a human-readable date.

articles.title: How source-generated P/Invoke decompiles
articles.excerpt: Decompile a method marked [DllImport] and you get almost nothing back: an extern signature, a reconstructed attribute, and no body. Decompile a method marked [LibraryImport] and you get a page of real…
articles.body: Decompile a method marked [DllImport] and you get almost nothing back: an extern signature, a reconstructed attribute, and no body. Decompile a method marked [LibraryImport] and you get a page of real C# — fixed blocks, pointer casts, a nested call. Same native call, wildly different decompiled output. The reason is where the marshalling code lives, and it is worth understanding, because it changes what you can learn from an assembly by reading it. The real question Both attributes describe the same thing: a managed method that is really a call across the native boundary. So why does one survive decompilation as an empty husk and the other as a fully readable method?

articles.title: Orchestrating Agents: What Strands Teaches About Workflow Determinism vs. LLM Freedom
articles.excerpt: Agent orchestration frameworks promise to tame LLM non-determinism by imposing execution order. Strands, an AWS-backed workflow tool, makes that trade explicit: you declare a dependency graph in Pytho…
articles.body: Agent orchestration frameworks promise to tame LLM non-determinism by imposing execution order. Strands, an AWS-backed workflow tool, makes that trade explicit: you declare a dependency graph in Python, and tasks run only when their upstream dependencies reach completed status. The model no longer decides who runs next. You do. But deterministic sequencing comes with a cost. Upstream results arrive as plain text spliced into the next step's prompt. No field names, no types, no validators. Each step is still a full agent loop, and the model inside it still decides which tools to call and what words to produce. Nine real production runs show what breaks when you split workflow control from data contracts.

articles.title: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 is approaching a distance of one light-day from Earth, a milestone that highlights the enormous distances involved in deep-space exploration.
articles.body: After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth. This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond. Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.

articles.title: 'Maybe the scariest thing I've heard in my life': Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover reveals his toughest challenge before flying to the moon
articles.excerpt: For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, one of the hardest parts of traveling to the moon happened before he even left Earth.
articles.body: TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters. Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet. "This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said.

articles.title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18! Here's what you need to know
articles.excerpt: The Leonid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 17-18, sending shooting stars racing across the night sky from the direction of the constellation Leo.
articles.body: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026!
